title: Three men sentenced to death in Jordan over church mass shooting
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Nine people were killed in the shooting at the Greek Orthodox church last monthByElla KiplingA Jordanian court has
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Nine people were killed in the shooting at the Greek Orthodox church last monthByElla KiplingA Jordanian court has sentenced three men to death by hanging for carrying out a fatal mass shooting on a church last month.The attack on 23 October killed nine people and injured 34 others who had been attending a Christian funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate.Jordan's Armed Forces said in a statement on Sunday that the men had been convicted of committing "terrorist acts", as well as possessing weapons, "promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation" and "conspiracy to commit terrorist acts". The three men - two Jordanian brothers and their brother-in-law - fled the scene of the attack and were arrested three days later. They have not been publicly identified.Karak is home to a sizeable Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom.CCTV footage from the day of the attack showed three men holding guns approaching and firing on St George's church in the village of Hmoud.Figure caption, Watch: CCTV footage appears to show gunmen near churchA second video showed dead and wounded people lying on the ground amid chaotic scenes at the church.It is still unclear why the attackers chose to target that specific church.Shortly after the attack, Jordan's King Abdullah II wrote on X: "The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation. "Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity."The three men fled the scene of the shooting and were later located inside an abandoned house in Karak governorate, south of the capital, Amman.They refused to surrender and opened fire on security forces, who returned fire and wounded all three of them, the Public Security Directorate said at the time. No security personnel were hurt in the shootout.King Abdullah praised security forces for chasing the suspects "to the very end".The week after the Karak shooting, Jordan struck what its military said were "terrorist organisations" in Syria in retaliation to the church attack.Syrian health officials told state media that five people, including women, children and an elderly man, were killed in the strike on a village in the southern Daraa province. Jordan said its fighter jets had killed and wounded "several terrorists" without giving further details.Jordan said it had co-ordinated with the Syrian government, but Syria said it had not been notified in advance.Executions in Jordan are carried out by hanging. The kingdom previously observed an unofficial ban on executions from 2006 to 2014, and another pause from 2017 until June this year.

schema.headline: Three men sentenced to death in Jordan over church mass shooting

title: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history'
description: Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of missiles and drones i
body: Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of missiles and drones in Ukraine airspace.The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back".It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented.The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher.On Sunday Zelensky said Ukraine was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones targeting electricity substations because "restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there"."Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161km/h (100mph) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds'," he posted, referring to the drones that follow an Iranian design.On Friday Zelensky said speed limits of around 100mph had been enforced on the network since Monday, but only in Russian-occupied areas and not the whole of Ukraine."It already has political implications. If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporary occupied territories as not ours," the New York Times reported him as saying.Ukraine has also been beset by a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors used to defend against Russian missiles - a situation that Russia has exploited to intensify strikes on Ukrainian targets.Overnight and into Sunday morning Russia hit energy infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and the Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr, and Kirovohrad regions, Ukraine said.It also struck railway infrastructure in the Dnipro, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions.Scores of people are said to have been hurt in those attacks, as well as two in the Donetsk and Kyiv regions.Two people were killed in an attack on an infrastructure facility in Chernihiv Region's Mena, governor Vyacheslav Chaus said.Multiple strikes were also delivered on energy facilities across the region, he added on Telegram.Ukraine meanwhile said it had carried out strikes on a petrochemical plant and an oil refinery in the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk."On the night of November 15, units of Ukraine's Defence Forces reached Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan," the military said on Telegram."Two enterprises that feed the Russian war with raw materials and fuel came under attack."Other Ukrainian strikes killed one person in Taganrog, an industrial port city near the border, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said.In the occupied Luhansk region a lorry driver and an elderly woman were also killed, Leonid Pasechnik, the regional leader installed by Moscow said.Meanwhile Estonia has announced it will shut its border crossing points with Russia from 1 December following a suspected sabotage attack on a defence company.Eight people were detained over an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.The Estonian authorities say they had been ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence service to try and carry out the attack. Russia has not commented."Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.

schema.headline: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history'

title: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
description: A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tool
body: A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated.The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation.Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance."I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday."I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating."When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam.He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly."It seems that because of me, other successful candidates are being suspected," he suggested.The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting after Han admitted cheating.The South Korean president's policy chief Ha Jun-kyung said new measures would be introduced to prevent cheating and warned "past crimes" would be "tracked down and apprehended to the very end".Those found to have used AI to cheat in the tax accountancy exam will have their qualification revoked and will be banned from retaking the test for five years, the government said.The scandal comes just days before the east Asian nation's annual college entrance exam, a crucial hurdle for students.

schema.headline: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating

title: Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack
description: Iran launched a drone attack against a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second attempt to target the country in three days.The country's Isl
body: Iran launched a drone attack against a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second attempt to target the country in three days.The country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted the US air defence radar facility at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain using six drones.Bahrain's military said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed the Iranian air attacks "before they could achieve their objectives".It comes after Iran fired drones at Bahrain on Friday, its first attack against Gulf countries since September. The US and Iran are locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows through it but shipping has been restricted since the outbreak of war in February.Iran insists that it should control the strait and has been attacking what it calls "unauthorised" traffic, while the US military is providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the strait to keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states.As sirens sounded across Bahrain on Sunday the interior ministry called on citizens to head to their nearest safe location.Bahrain's foreign ministry said: "The Kingdom of Bahrain condemns in the strongest terms the continued brutal Iranian attacks on its territory and holds Iran fully responsible for their consequences."In a statement on the strikes shared by Iran's state broadcaster on Telegram, the IRGC said: "The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response."Earlier this week, the IRGC claimed that it struck a US early warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday.The US military has denied the claim, stating that the IRGC launched two one-way attack drones towards Bahrain and both were shot down by US forces. It added that there were no injuries or damage. Earlier in the week the US carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials told CBS, the BBC's US partner.The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait.The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a naval blockade of Iranian ports.Iranian negotiators had been discussing with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US meets seven conditions, reportedly including the lifting of the naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian assets.However this week Donald Trump said that the US was no longer interested in a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered Vice-President JD Vance, who had been involved in efforts to restart negotiations, to focus on domestic US politics.

schema.headline: Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack

title: CJP: India’s protesters face government crackdown after summer victory
description: After a summer win, India's Gen Z protesters face a winter of uncertaintyFigure caption, India's Gen Z protesters are facing the limits of dissentByAz
body: After a summer win, India's Gen Z protesters face a winter of uncertaintyFigure caption, India's Gen Z protesters are facing the limits of dissentByAzadeh MoshiriSouth Asia Correspondent, DelhiCheers erupted at Delhi's Jantar Mantar protest site in July as news broke that Gen-Z protests had forced federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign. One protester turned to me, beaming: "This is the youth's victory."Just over three months later, the mood has shifted dramatically. Student protesters are now struggling even to assemble. Demonstrations by the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) last month over voting rights were met with sweeping restrictions and thousands of peaceful protesters were detained.The summer had seen a new wave of dissent in India, driven by deep frustration among the youth and fuelled by irreverent online satire. The movement spread across the country, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a leader with a strongman image, unaccustomed to open criticism or mockery, struggled to contain it. But the government's increasingly forceful security response suggests it has learned from its rare concession to protesters, invoking public order to curb dissent.The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national spokesperson Syed Zafar Islam rejected accusations of heavy-handedness and told the BBC: "The right to protest and freedom of expression is mandated by the constitution, but it has to be done within the law. It cannot override the rights of others, at the cost of public security".This is by no means the first time the Modi government has faced large-scale protests. But the breadth of them pose a challenge for the BJP, according to Yamini Aiyar, former president of the Centre for Policy Research and visiting professor at Brown University.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The CJP led massive protests in July which ended with the resignation of a federal minister"They are not defined by caste, gender or economic class," Aiyar said. "Even some of the core BJP base, the upwardly mobile, lower-income classes, were attracted by the movement."The scale of the youth protests is also magnified by its online presence. Protesters have broken a longstanding political taboo, openly mocking the prime minister online."It's more than just laughs," said Sakhi, a student protester who identifies as they/them and affiliated with one of Delhi University's left-wing student organisations."The fear of repercussions in other generations isn't felt as much in ours," they said. "Comedy is a new language to challenge authority."Previous protest movements posed serious challenges to Modi but were easier to dismiss as representing narrow sections of society or to label "anti-national", according to Aiyar.In 2020, farmers protesting against controversial agricultural reforms were blocked from entering Delhi, leading to months of demonstrations and, at times, clashes on the capital's borders. After a year of protests, the government abandoned the reforms.Protests against a contentious citizenship law in 2019 and 2020 are a stark reminder of the powers of the judiciary should anyone be deemed a national security threat.Student activist Umar Khalid was arrested under anti-terror laws after violent clashes in Delhi that killed 53 people, mostly Muslims. He was accused of being a "key conspirator". He has now spent more than six years in jail without his trial having begun.His partner Banojyotsna Lahiri told the BBC they have no regrets, but that the situation instilled "a kind of fear that has prevailed".Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty ImagesImage caption, The CJP in its early days became a unifier for Indian youth frustrated with the state of education, jobs and economy "We are just looking at a very dark mesh of empty space, because we don't know when the endpoint is," Lahiri said. Khalid's latest appeal was lodged this month.Aiyar believes opponents are using a familiar "playbook" today to "de-legitimise" protests, but that it isn't resonating as convincingly.Nevertheless, the youth protests have struggled to recapture this summer's momentum.CJP leaders, including spokesperson Saurav Das, have faced repeated detentions and legal action. Das and fellow leader Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in Delhi's Tihar jail after being accused of trespassing at Jantar Mantar. The site of their summer victory has since been struck off the list of authorised protest venues, a decision being challenged in court.Protesters from other groups, including the left-wing All India Students' Association (Aisa), have also faced police action over allegations of defying orders."We were expecting some kind of crackdown," said Das. He added that "the government has learnt a lot" since the summer.Legal experts warn the proceedings themselves can have a chilling effect."A lot of cases can lead to acquittals, but it can take years. The process is the punishment, and that can deter protesters," said Ali Khan, an assistant professor at Lloyd Law College.The restrictions on demonstrations have become excessive, according to constitutional lawyer Vrinda Grover, who is advising the CJP.Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty ImageImage caption, Tens of thousands of people gathered at Delhi's iconic Ramlila Maidan for the opposition protest on 1 November"Those who are organising the protests have repeatedly emphasised that this is non-violent," she argued. "Rights have been whittled down in the name of law and order."The BJP has rejected suggestions it is suppressing peaceful dissent.Islam told the BBC that demonstrations "cannot override the rights of other citizens just because a handful of people want to protest and be responsible for violence".Even dissenting online carries risk. Sakhi's viral social media posts have attracted targeted abuse and transphobic attacks. The BBC has seen posts threatening them with violence and rape.Sometimes, it can deter Sakhi from protesting or even make them change the way they dress."Making people laugh can turn into being called anti-national," Sakhi said. "They want me to feel damaged," they added.They claim some of their content was removed after getting millions of views.Under India's information technology laws, the government can order platforms to block content on national security grounds. Notices on X and Instagram have shown accounts being withheld in India.CJP leaders have likened the crackdown to the 1975 Emergency, when then prime minister Indira Gandhi suspended civil liberties and jailed political opponents.Yet dissent has not been stamped out.Opposition parties have, in part, filled the void. Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi on 1 November for a rally organised by INDIA bloc, an alliance of opposition parties led by Congress, and permitted by the authorities.CJP leaders, meanwhile, insist the movement is bigger than their organisation.When Das walked out Delhi's Tihar prison on 21 October, photographs showed him smiling."I would just say wait and watch," Das told us. "Time is on our side. We are a very young generation."

schema.headline: CJP: India’s protesters face government crackdown after summer victory

title: Judo champion Teddy Riner shakes up French presidential race with surprise candidacy
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Five-times Olympic champion Teddy Riner is one of France's most popular athletesByHugh SchofieldIn ParisApart from
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Five-times Olympic champion Teddy Riner is one of France's most popular athletesByHugh SchofieldIn ParisApart from an overwhelming urge to pin one's opponent to the floor of the house, there is no obvious connection between politics and the world of top-level judo.That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race.The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances.Riner is, after all, one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, regularly topping the polls for embodying the nation's "values". He is a proven winner, with five Olympic golds and 11 world championships under his belt, as well as a successful career in business.More than 28 million people have watched his election broadcast on Instagram and X, shot with proper presidential decorum against a backdrop of books and a French flag. Some 22% told an Ifop poll within 24 hours they "could" vote for him.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Teddy Riner's video has attracted 14.5 million views on Instagram aloneActors and television personalities have become presidents in other countries. The ex-leader of Liberia – George Weah – was formerly a professional footballer.So why not a judoka in the Élysée Palace?"Anyone who thinks that being out of the political in-crowd disqualifies Riner from running for the Élysée would be very wrong," says Guillaume Tabard of Le Figaro."But [Riner] too would be wrong if he thinks not belonging to the in-crowd is all it takes."For now the whole of the French political world has decided to take the Riner candidacy seriously – or at least to pretend to. That is partly because he is such a popular personality that mocking his political hopes could easily rebound badly.But it is also because the state of French politics – outside of the burgeoning forces of the hard left and hard right – is one of total disarray.The centre-ground is floundering, with no candidate yet emerging who can inspire anything like the sense of mission of hard-right leader Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the hard left, who for now look set to face off in the final round of the presidential election in May.So when a popular figure like Riner enters the race - proclaiming himself "neither left, nor right", wanting to "unite the country" and "put money back in people's pockets", railing equally against "racists" and "yobs who scare people off our streets" – politicians have to take note.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Hard-right leader Marine Le Pen currently leads the polls in the race to be France's next presidentIt is perfectly possible, probable even, that Riner's campaign will fizzle out after a brief period of hype, and that the judoka will after all be a joker in the pack. But it is also possible that it won't, in which case the pre-election arithmetic will need a hasty readjustment: and it won't be the centrists who are smiling.Thus far, Riner has shown himself a master of the codes required for this kind of out-of-nowhere candidacy, the first of which is to press home the message: "Don't Worry! I'm NOT a Politician!"In this day and age in France, anyone who smacks of the "system" is automatically downgraded in voters' eyes, so it is important to emphasise that you are only running for office because, one, you have experienced real life (unlike those loafers in Paris); and two, you have discovered that there are solutions out there for the country's many problems. Solutions that are invisible to those same blinkered apparatchiks.All this Riner was able to express in last Monday's social media broadcast by using sophisticated rhetorical devices."People say I am a fool for wanting to run for the presidency," he said."Am I a fool? Well, if refusing to see France sink under the weight of debt; refusing to see mothers and fathers grit their teeth every time they do their weekly shop, and tremble with fear when their kids go out on the street… if all that means being a fool, then yes call me a fool."It was a promising oratorial start for the sportsman, and certainly attracted the viewers. But if he is serious – and Riner says he never does anything half-heartedly - that's not how he became an Olympic champion – then the hard work begins now.What does Riner actually want to do? Who will be on his team? Where does he position himself on the all-consuming matters of the day: pension-reform,  investment in education, the cost of living, public debt, the rise of populism or Russia's war in Ukraine?In short, how does he intend to transform his undeniable popularity as a sporting figure into a political mandate?Image source, ReutersImage caption, Protesters have for weeks taken to the streets in France over wages, the cost of living and public services Broadly, Riner appears to be on the right on economic matters and law and order, but being black and of Caribbean background he is also very strong on racism. When he says he is anti-extremism, he is referring mainly to Marine Le Pen.In other words his pitch is somewhere in the centre, and against the extremes.The trouble is, this is already an extremely crowded area, with important figures like ex-prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal signally failing to take off.Currently there are a dozen or so candidates in the area between centre right and centre left, stretching from the Socialist-backed Raphaël Glucksman to the Republicans' Bruno Retailleau on the right.The latest possible addition is Christine Lagarde, who steps down as head of the European Central Bank next February.Image source, Pool/AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, President Emmanuel Macron is among the few politicians who appears genuinely pleased by Riner's decision to runThe addition of yet another contender will dilute their polling numbers even further, making a second-round qualification for Mélenchon more likely.So no wonder the leader of France Unbowed (LFI) seemed so happy about Riner's decision to run. "We know how it goes: neither right nor left means not left," Mélenchon told reporters on Friday.The only other politician who seems genuinely pleased, rather than putting on a fixed smile, is President Emmanuel Macron, who said Riner was a "great champion" and that politics "did not belong to the professionals".That could be explained by the president's cool relations with his former prime ministers, Philippe and Attal, both of whom are doing all they can to distance themselves from their unpopular one-time boss.Riner said he viewed Macron's praise as a "poisoned chalice", telling reporters on Saturday that he was "not the president's envoy, I'm not a Macronist".Politics and judo have very little in common, but of the two, as Riner will soon discover, the more vicious is not the one that is fought out hand-to-hand after mutual acknowledgement on the tatami mat. In Japanese, judo actually means "the gentle way".If he starts looking like a serious candidate, Riner must know his life will be turned upside down, not just his physical form. In politics you do not bow in respect to your opponent. You give him a metaphorical headbutt.

schema.headline: Judo champion Teddy Riner shakes up French presidential race with surprise candidacy

title: Thousands of US flights cancelled or delayed two days after grounding of planes nationwide
description: Thousands of US flights were cancelled or delayed on Sunday as the US air-traffic control system continued to recover from a technical failure that le
body: Thousands of US flights were cancelled or delayed on Sunday as the US air-traffic control system continued to recover from a technical failure that led to a rare national ground stop.Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said normal operations may not be restored until Monday. "We have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time," he told the BBC's US partner CBS. More than 5,000 flights were delayed and 2,000 cancelled on Sunday.President Donald Trump urged Congress on Sunday to approve more money to modernise the air-traffic control system. The grounding of all aircraft scheduled to depart the US on Friday caused chaos at airports across the country.More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the FAA announced at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) that flights would be grounded until further notice. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.In the aftermath, 8,500 flights were delayed and another 8,000 cancelled, according to FlightAware.The stoppage left passengers stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to their gates. Others were stranded in airports, sleeping on the floor and desperately trying to get in touch with their airline. The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.The ground stop was lifted after about four and a half hours, but the impacts continued over the weekend.On Saturday, airlines cancelled more than 5,900 flights and more than 7,000 others were delayed.Investigators are still working to determine the root cause and who is at fault, but Duffy said the administration decided to ground flights after failures in a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate.   The transport secretary said a computer router installed as part of an upgrade from copper wire to fibre started sending out faulty signals. He said on Sunday that the router - a piece of equipment which directs traffic across the network - was installed in El Dorado, Arkansas, and "flooded our network". Duffy said that issues will continue to arise until the US makes major modernising changes to its air control system. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said."Let's not lie to each other," he said on NBC's Meet The Press. "We have to make investments into a network that has been neglected for decades."In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump urged US lawmakers to allocate the money, saying "we can get it built quickly and efficiently"."It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS! We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs," he said. Experts say the US uses antiquated technology for flight communications. Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."

schema.headline: Thousands of US flights cancelled or delayed two days after grounding of planes nationwide

title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
description: Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year,
body: Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the  company says.Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.It said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips. Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

schema.headline: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says

title: Ebola in DR Congo: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola.
description: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can surviveImage source, Braton Serge/BBCByRuth AlongaBBC AfricaReporti
body: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can surviveImage source, Braton Serge/BBCByRuth AlongaBBC AfricaReporting fromButemboWhen Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there."Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience."As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works.The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate.Image source, Braton Serge/BBCImage caption, Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga uses his book to help convince sceptics that Ebola is realThe first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team.After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve.Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north.This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance.After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea.This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre."She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says.Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance.He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids.Image caption, Dr Kamwanga's mother says his experience has helped dispel some of the misinformation she had heard about EbolaThe current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment."The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea.In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding.Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified."I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains.Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok.The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him.However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged."We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC.For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region.He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance.Neighbour Kavugho Sifa shared these concerns."We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC.They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola. Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation.After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust."I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact." During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real.But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding.Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says."Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate".He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion.But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone.Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community.He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly."He agrees too with the recent report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing."The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says.The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease."Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited."More from the BBC on the Ebola crisis:

title: What we know about the US ground stop and what to do if your flight is affected
description: On Friday afternoon, a government contractor called L3Harris was continuing work on upgrading an aviation telecoms network. As it swapped out copper l
body: On Friday afternoon, a government contractor called L3Harris was continuing work on upgrading an aviation telecoms network. As it swapped out copper lines for fibre at a remote location in the US, L3Harris installed a router - a piece of equipment which basically directs traffic across the network.According to Duffy, that router started flooding others in the air traffic control system, sending 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds.As a result, 17 out of 22 air route traffic control centres in the US experienced "instability" on voice and ground communications, said Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). It took the aviation authority 45 minutes to identify where the problem was because maintenance is logged manually on paper.This meant the FAA had to "pore through" the physical documents "to figure out who's working on what", Bedford admitted.As a precaution as it tried to track down the cause, Bedford said the decision was made to ground all flights.Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".  He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."Duffy said the system needed a complete overhaul, estimating a $50bn price tag.In the meantime, he said authorities would work to determine whether it was "incompetence" or faulty equipment that led to the outage. He also said there would be "re-evaluation" of allowing upgrades to be done during the day. In a statement on Saturday afternoon, L3Harris confirmed it was working with the FAA to modernise the airspace communications infrastructure and said it was supporting the agency with its investigation. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," the firm said. Juliette Kayyem, US assistant secretary of Homeland Security under President Barack Obama, questioned why an upgrade was done on one of the week's busiest days for travel."You don't do it on a Friday when there's lots of air traffic controllers," she said"You try to find ways to minimise its upgrade so you're not maybe doing it across the board in a single moment but you also have to have systems that are ready to step in if the upgrade in any way begins to threaten the system," Kayyem added.A spokesperson for L3Harris said is it "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop of our nation's air travel".He added: "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."All US-bound air traffic from Eurocontrol member states was suspended.There are 42 Eurocontrol member states, including dozens of EU nations, the UK and Turkey, as well as Israel and Morocco.Passengers travelling from the UK have been warned of possible disruption on Saturday morning.A number of flights to the US from Heathrow airport were cancelled and delayed, but Manchester airport said no significant disruption was expected. Flights were operating as normal from Gatwick airport.Australia's largest international airport, Sydney, had grounded all US-bound flights, but scheduled flights are now expected to depart as planned.Air Canada also cancelled flights between the US and Canada.Duffy said on Saturday: "We are back at full operations."But, as he predicted on Friday, it is taking time to unwind what happened. FlightAware said more than 5,900 flights were cancelled and more than 7,000 delayed in the US on Saturday. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines said they were resuming operations but they both cancelled 20% of their flights on Saturday. American Airlines cancelled 520 journeys.Meanwhile, JetBlue cancelled 40% of its scheduled journeys.By Sunday morning, the situation had improved, but the impacts of the stoppage were still being felt with more than 2,400 flights delayed and 1,400 cancelled.In the US, UK and the EU, airlines may be liable for compensation if the reason for a delay is deemed within their control, such as a fault with the plane or pilot sickness.As such, airlines do not have to provide compensation to passengers for air traffic control problems.But passengers are still protected to a certain degree under US federal - and country-specific - laws. Under the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, cancelled or "significantly delayed flights" - defined as three hours for domestic flights and six hours for international routes - must be offered alternative travel or a full refund of the fare if the passenger chooses not to fly. It also requires all air carriers to issue refunds for tickets purchased with credit cards within seven business days of the request, and 20 days for tickets purchased with another form of payment. Passengers accepting a new flight cannot receive a refund.In the US, there is no requirement for airlines to provide meal vouchers or accommodation, but some may offer complimentary support to customers. However, if passengers are travelling from the UK to the US or flying with a UK carrier, you may have additional rights. Under UK law, airlines have a duty to look after you when flights are delayed or cancelled for whatever reason.This includes:a reasonable amount of food and drink (often through vouchers)a way for you to communicate (often by refunding the cost of calls)free accommodation, if you have to stay overnight to fly the next daytransport to and from that accommodationIf your airline is unable to arrange assistance, you have the right to organise this yourself and claim back the cost later.The Civil Aviation Authority advises people to keep receipts and not spend more than necessary.It was only the second such nationwide stoppage since the immediate aftermath of the al-Qaeda plane hijackings of 11 September 2001."This looks like the worst since 9/11, but clearly not on that scale," Dr Guy Gratton, an associate professor of aviation at Cranfield University, told BBC Verify.Gratton pointed to a US grounding in 2023 due to a failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system."That lasted 1 hour and 52 minutes, delayed about 9,500 flights and cancelled about 1,300," he said.The 2023 outage meant air traffic safety notices could no longer be published and flights were grounded until that system was restored.

title: Czechs rally against plan to switch funding of public media
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Organisers said around 400,000 people took part on Sunday ByRachel FlynnUpdated 3 hours agoThousands of peopl
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Organisers said around 400,000 people took part on Sunday ByRachel FlynnUpdated 3 hours agoThousands of people have gathered in central Prague to protest against the Czech government's plans to scrap the licence fee and use the state budget to fund public media.Critics say the plans would allow politicians to stifle media freedom.The coalition government - which consists of the populist ANO party and two right-wing Eurosceptic parties - insists the change will not affect editorial independence, but wants broadcasters to cut costs.Parliament passed the first draft of the proposal late last month. Since then, thousands of Czechs have taken part in protests.Czech households currently pay ⁠205 crowns ($9.44; £7.06) a month for public TV and radio. Sunday's protest was organised by the Million Moments for Democracy association which said "roughly 400,000" people had attended."I know that our entire Czech Television is a guarantee of truth and objectivity," pensioner Milana Rudolfova, 72, told Reuters news agency. "If we do not have public television and radio then unfortunately we will not be able to believe anything anymore."Image source, EPAImage caption, The protesters say the planned changes could allow politicians to stifle media freedomPrime Minister Andrej Babis has insisted the government does not want to control public media. "The funding system is changing, no one wants to control public media, no one wants to dictate to them what they should say and do, no one wants to nationalise them," Babis told the Czech News Agency. "We are doing this because the system is already outdated and most of Europe is going the same way today and others are joining in," he added. Some European countries, including France and Norway, have moved away from the public licence fee model in the last few years.France removed it in 2022 and its public media, which also carries advertising, is now funded by a portion of the income from VAT. Norway abolished its license fee in 2020 and moved its public broadcaster's funding into the national budget.Image source, EPAImage caption, These protesters held a sign depicting the animated character Vecernicek and saying "We stand with Czech TV"Some protesters wore pointed hats folded out of newspapers as a tribute to an animated character, Vecernicek, who has introduced Czech Television's nightly children's bedtime stories for decades.Critics have compared the government's media bill to changes in Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who tightly controlled state media when he was in power.Prime Minister Andrej Babis was appointed in December in 2025, and has faced criticism over his coalition's attacks on Czech media."Political attacks against private and public media have become one of the hallmarks of Andrej Babis' premiership," said Pavol Szalai, Prague Bureau director of international press freedom organisation Reporters Without Borders, in June.

schema.headline: Czechs rally against plan to switch funding of public media

title: Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?
description: ByVictoria GillScience correspondentIn 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.Until that moment, the 11-year-
body: ByVictoria GillScience correspondentIn 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him.More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary – but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla – that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward."He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma.Figure caption, Jojo's keeper Maxe Anaclet Makaba: 'He definitely feels lonely - you can see it in his eyes'Jojo was less than a year old – an infant clinging to his mother – when he was captured and sold.Most gorillas spend the first 14 to 19 years of their life in an embedded family unit but he was kept completely alone and on public display at the private zoo that bought him.Maxe Anaclet Makaba, who is head keeper at Lekedi and sees Jojo nearly every day, says it is clear he "craves human interaction"."He will even go to the trouble of gathering leaves for us to hold, so that we [trade them] for a treat – to interact with us," he says.Jojo also calls out when women he knows well visit his enclosure and then leave, making sounds that silverback males use to summon the females in the wild, explains Éric Willaume, who runs the sanctuary."He definitely feels lonely," he says.Image caption, When Jojo first arrived at the sanctuary after spending years in a small iron cage, he didn't look directly at peopleJojo is one of the more than 6,000 African primates estimated to have been bought or sold in the global trade of apes and other primates between 2000 and 2023. Thousands more are trafficked illegally for use as exotic pets, wild meat, and traditional medicine, the Pan African Sanctuary Alliance says., externalExperts believe when baby great apes are taken from their group at a young age like Jojo, they are left traumatised."If they're old enough to understand what happened to them, to understand their family was killed, they just lose the will to live," explains conservationist Tony King, from UK charity the Aspinall Foundation. "You see it in their eyes – the light goes out. I never knew where that expression came from, but I've seen it in gorillas."King – who specialises in rehabilitating rescued great apes – remembers rescuing two infant sister gorillas who were brought to a sanctuary in the Congo Basin. "They were clinging to each other," he says. "They stayed together in a little tight ball for about three days before they sort of unravelled. I think that's what kept them alive."Image source, Sinead Lynch/The Aspinall FoundationImage caption, Sisters Likendze and Matoko clutch each other after they were brought in a wooden crate to the Project Protection des Gorilles sanctuary in the CongoAfrican charity the Gorilla Rehabilitation and Conservation Education (Grace) Center uses what it calls "gorilla-led" rehabilitation. When the team rescues a young gorilla from the pet trade, they put it with a group as soon as possible so they can socialise and essentially learn to be a gorilla.But Jojo's case is unusual. He is fully mature and showing signs of harmful, chronic stress, according to Forrester.In a game-changing approach to studying anxiety and trauma in apes, she has used a thermal camera to film Jojo's face. This allows her to monitor blood flow, revealing what appears to be a chronically cold nose.It's a sign of a malfunctioning stress response. When any primate – a human, chimp or gorilla - is stressed, blood flow to the eyes and ears increases. It puts them on high alert for danger, but leaves their nose, temporarily, colder. For Jojo, this "nasal dip" as it is known, does not seem to recover."Being connected to others is incredibly important to our psychology as great apes," Forrester says. "Having another individual to share his life with would be so healing for him."I would assume other gorillas would help him process this grief and trauma."Image source, G ForresterImage caption, Thermal imaging of Jojo's face reveals signs of chronic stress, with a persistently cold nose indicating a potentially disrupted stress responseDr Katie Fawcett, from the Grace Center, says it's also "essential" for an animal to form social relationships to be considered for release into the wild - which is the ultimate goal for Jojo's keepers.The bonds between gorillas – what we would call friendship - is key to their society, adds Dr Robin Morrison from the University of Zurich, who studies the social lives of mountain gorillas. In one recent study, she discovered that female mountain gorillas would seek out females they knew, even if they hadn't seen them for many years, when joining a group.And she says a big part of a gorilla's normal social life is "just sitting together quietly sharing space".But Jojo has never been given the opportunity to sit quietly with another gorilla.No one knows how Jojo will react to a companion. Moving an animal from an accredited zoo would be a decision for an international committee and based on genetics, health and the animals' personalities and compatibility.Any introduction to another animal would be done very carefully – perhaps giving them an object that smells of the other before they see each other. These slow, cautious ape introductions do happen – when an animal moves from one zoo group to another, for example. Forrester has contacted a number of accredited zoos to explore the possibility of doing this for Jojo. But those discussions have fizzled out with no sign of progress.The problem, she says, is "there aren't clear processes in place to do these kinds of trans-locations".Image source, Dian Fossey Gorilla FundImage caption, Encounters between two or more separate gorilla groups are complex social eventsThe international rules and processes for moving captive gorillas across international borders - from one zoo or safari park to another - are designed for breeding programmes."They're not designed for reintroductions into the wild, or to find companions for animals that might need them," says Forrester.And because Jojo, who is probably in his 20s, has reached maturity, King thinks it might be too late for him to bond with other gorillas."Jojo's situation is unique, but he is probably best where he is," King says, adding that introducing him to another animal could, somewhat ironically, be a source of more stress for him.Image source, G ForresterImage caption, Prof Forrester studies Jojo as part of research to understand how our understanding of human mental health - particularly stress and trauma - can be applied to our great ape relativesBeing alone is also natural, even relatively common, for mature male gorillas. According to Morrison, about a third of adult males are solitary. "When they reach adolescence, they tend to disperse and spend a good chunk of their life on their own."Solo males will try to persuade females to form a group with them, but some don't succeed and may feel lonely as a consequence, Morrison believes. "If we think of loneliness in an evolutionary context - this mismatch between the social interactions they want and the social interactions they're getting. I suspect feeling lonely is part of the natural, evolutionary drive to attract females."But while those phases – of family life and adult solitude - play a role in wild gorilla society, Jojo was forced into solitary confinement as an infant.Morrison believes Jojo is probably both traumatised and lonely."[In the wild] gorillas move together, find food together, sleep together," she says. "So much of their lives is just being with this group."That is what Jojo's keepers, Forrester, and others want for Jojo. A friend. Maybe a female, or a compatible male."It would be good for him to have a companion," says keeper Makaba. "Because being alone is like being cut off from the world - it's like being in prison. "Having another gorilla there would be a good thing for him."GorillasGabonEnvironmentPrimates

schema.headline: Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?

title: Judge blocks Trump closure of 'Trash Island' Washington DC golf course
description: A federal judge has temporarily blocked the US government's closure of an historic golf course and park in Washington DC. US District Judge Ana Reyes
body: A federal judge has temporarily blocked the US government's closure of an historic golf course and park in Washington DC. US District Judge Ana Reyes has been overseeing a months-long challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links, which he said would be closed from 15 November for extensive renovations.Reyes has said President Donald Trump cannot close the park nor its golf course, but added that his administration was not required to actively manage either.Trump, an avid golfer, has said his plans to upgrade the 106-year-old course will create "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World". The BBC has contacted the White House for comment. Declaring the current course "Trash Island", he announced in October that it would be renovated over 15 months to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments" - despite the ongoing litigation.Reyes said in a 30-page decision issued on Saturday that the Trump administration's justifications for the proposed course closures were pretextual and that the government had violated at least two federal laws "to meet an arbitrary deadline"."The government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely," Reyes wrote.She said the closure "runs counter to the public interest in utilising national parkland", adding that the government had not "plausibly identified any harm it would suffer from a temporary restraining order that preserves the status quo pending further proceedings".Her order will last until 28 November.A coalition of advocacy and legal groups opposing the closure and renovation said they are "grateful that the court has stopped the government from unlawfully closing East Potomac Park and depriving people of this priceless piece of American history and wonderful recreation space". "Our laws prevent this administration from acting without a fair and public process, and today's order will stop the government from ignoring those laws," said the coalition, which represents the plaintiffs and includes Democracy Forward and the Democracy Defenders Fund. "We are eager to continue to argue this case in court."The legal dispute dates back to February, when the DC Preservation League and others sued over redevelopment plans for the park.The historic course, which sits two miles (3km) south of the White House, is one of three public courses run by the National Park Service (NPS) in the nation's capital.The legal fight then escalated in October when the NPS began to cut down hundreds of trees without notifying Reyes until 15 hours before work was set to begin. After the trees were cut, Reyes ordered the Trump administration to stop tree removal until at least 26 October and give her three business days' notice about making any other permanent changes. Despite the work stoppage, Trump announced that the course would be closed for 15 months from 15 November to accommodate for the renovations. He also shared a rendering of the course redesign."The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous and disease-infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall," he said in a post on Truth Social.Reyes has since separately opened an inquiry into whether justice department attorneys had "made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated ethical rules".That included whether giving late notice to the court about the renovation plans had been "done in bad faith", and whether the attorneys failed to correct previously false statements or withheld information.She said she would carry out the inquiry with a special master, an independent third party.

schema.headline: Judge blocks Trump closure of 'Trash Island' Washington DC golf course

title: Watch: SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket on return to Earth
description: SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket on its return to Earth for the first time."Can you believe it?," a commentator
body: SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket on its return to Earth for the first time."Can you believe it?," a commentator said as large crowds cheered at the launch site in Texas.The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday. The booster was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.The top part, known as the Ship, returned to Earth a few minutes behind schedule at around 15:20 local time (21:20 GMT) on Saturday, in the first-ever successful catch attempt.Read more on this story: SpaceX successfully catches top of huge Starship rocket for first time

schema.headline: Watch: SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket on return to Earth

title: Watch: Pope Leo rides in helicopter cockpit during Peru trip
description: Pope Leo XIV shared a cockpit with pilots from the Peruvian Air Force during his tour of Latin America.Sharing the video to social media, the force sa
body: Pope Leo XIV shared a cockpit with pilots from the Peruvian Air Force during his tour of Latin America.Sharing the video to social media, the force said having the Pope join its pilots on Saturday was "an honour and an unforgettable memory".On Sunday, the pontiff arrived in Cusco, a southern Andes Mountains city that was once the heart of the Inca empire.There, the Pope visited an ancient Inca fortress, where he said religious traditions could help counter an age marked by "divisions, wounds, mistrust," stressing that faith should unite people and bring them together "in the light of faith and love."The Peruvian leg of his tour holds special significance for the Pope.He not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.Read more on the significance of the Pope's visit to Peru
